Thanks Jonas — reviewed the attachment and the incident window.

Notes / decision:
- Eligibility: Starlite's reported 49-minute outage in a 30-day billing month would reduce availability below 99.9% by our SLA definition (we calculate % availability across total minutes). Per our standard policy, this is eligible for a service credit.
- Calculation approach: We typically compute the credit as a percentage of the monthly service fee proportional to the availability shortfall. For a 49-minute outage in a 30-day month (43,200 minutes) the availability loss is ~0.113% which maps to the credit tier that aligns with our SOW (see spreadsheet).
- Recommended credit: Offer the customer the computed credit (spreadsheet attached) and issue it as an invoice-level credit within 30 days once customer acknowledges. No additional approvals required for credits <= 15% of monthly committed spend.

Next steps for Jonas: 1) send the customer the calculation and the proposed credit amount, 2) confirm their billing contact and PO/ref to apply the credit, 3) if they accept, route to billing (cc Marissa) to create the credit memo.

Evelyn

Hi Maya / Tom,

Thanks again for flagging this. We reviewed the incident and the attached calculation shows the draft credit we propose under the SLA. Summary below:

- Incident window we used: 2026-07-28 14:03–14:52 UTC (49 minutes)
- Monthly window assumed: July 2026 (30 days = 43,200 minutes)
- Availability loss: 49 / 43,200 = 0.113%
- Contract mapping: per SOW, availability shortfall in this range corresponds to a credit equal to 10% of the monthly committed service fee
- Your monthly committed fee (per DL-72931): $100,000 -> proposed credit = $10,000

I've attached the calculation workbook for transparency ("sla-credit-calculation-2026-07-28.xlsx"). If that aligns with your records, please reply to confirm the acceptance and provide the billing reference (PO# or invoice #) you want the credit applied to. Once we have your go-ahead, we'll route to billing and aim to issue the credit within 30 days.
